newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF's Marchelli says against too strong euro start.
newsitem.headline: BoF's Marchelli says against too strong euro start.

text.p: Paul Marchelli, a member of the Bank of France's monetary policy council, said on Tuesday it would be a mistake to launch European monetary union with a euro which was too strong compared to the dollar at the start.

In an interview with Reuters, he also said that conditions were in place for a French interest rate cut as soon as possible. This could be done without upsetting the franc. The dollar was undervalued against European currencies, he added.
"We could quite easily give ourselves some autonomy in managing interest rates," he said.
"The sooner the better seems the best solution to me. All conditions are in place for us to make this cut," he said.

Marchelli, believed to be in a minority in the monetary policy council in favour of faster interest rate cuts, said that he thought France could cut rates even below those of Germany without upsetting the franc-mark exchange rate.

He said his view that French rates could be cut without hitting the franc against the mark differentiated him from former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who last week called for a sharp depreciation in the franc.
He declined to say by how much he thought the Bank of France's intervention rate should be cut. But the franc was solid and a rate cut "should not make the franc fall".
A debate in France which started last week among politicians over the value of the franc was essentially, he said, about the appropriate level for the euro against the dollar.
"The dollar is undervalued" compared to most European currencies, he said, echoing a line often reiterated by the government.
"We are seeing the start of the big debate on what the dollar-euro parity will be," Marchelli, one of nine members of the council in the independent central bank, said.
"That is the big question," he added.

He said he believed that the euro would be a very strong currency in the future, but "it would be a mistake to try to have a euro which is as strong as possible at the start," since this would damage European economies.

Asked whether he favoured a proposal floated by some politicians that the euro should be at parity with the dollar -- which would imply a big devaluation in the euro -- he said this "would be a good thing".
Europe had to push for a better parity against the dollar.
"The debate is only just beginning. The discussion is open."
Europe's mass unemployed would not accept a European monetary union launched with a euro which was too strong.
"Europe will only be made by the people...people today are asking questions, because they fear a Europe of the unemployed," he said.
